```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse=TRUE,comment="#>",fig.width=7,fig.height=4)
bench <- function(file) read.csv(system.file("benchmarks",file,package="sheepdog"),
                                 stringsAsFactors=FALSE,check.names=FALSE)
has_plot <- requireNamespace("ggplot2",quietly=TRUE)
library(dplyr)
cur <- bench("curiango-nested-metrics.csv")
ci <- bench("curiango-paired-bootstrap.csv")
night <- bench("curiango-nightly-summary.csv")
sim <- bench("multispecies-results.csv")
paired <- bench("multispecies-paired.csv")
changes <- bench("multispecies-changes.csv")
fmt <- function(x) formatC(x,format="f",digits=4)
scenario_names <- c(global="Global",species="Species differences",
                     site_species="Site × species differences")
```

This page collects what the calibration benchmarks tell us about predictive
performance, downstream sensitivity and computing time. It includes real
single-species data from the Curiango study and a multispecies simulation
with known truth. **Neither benchmark shows a consistent advantage of
`one_se_logloss` over `best_auc`.** The default favours probability scores
and simpler models; it is not a promise that every dataset will improve.

Following the style of [crywolf's performance article](https://provetelab.org/crywolf/articles/performance.html),
the page reports measured results, practical choices and limitations. The
scripts are in `dev/benchmarks/` in the source repository. Tables used here
are cached in `inst/benchmarks/`; building the vignette never downloads data
or re-runs hundreds of model fits.

## Real data: the Curiango study

The [Zenodo v2 deposit](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21795898) accompanying
Piatti et al.'s Curiango manuscript supplies
manually annotated three-second windows and classifier scores. We used
2,939 BirdNET and 8,032 custom-classifier windows with score ≥ 0.10, from
seven physical sites. Files were checked against Zenodo MD5 checksums;
data attribution follows the deposit's CC BY 4.0 licence.

The full survey table has 458,520 rows but only **97,806 distinct one-minute
recordings and 1,753 site-nights**. The deposit description says 97,906
recordings; these analyses use the count actually read. Repeated rows
were aggregated to the maximum score per classifier and recording before
counting nightly detections. Counts are recordings, not raw table rows.

### Candidates for one species

Through 3.1.0, the default multispecies family left only the global model
estimable for this one-species dataset; the four species-effect models
failed. From 3.2.0, `calibrate()` and
`compare_calibration_models()` choose the following family automatically
when only one species is observed:

```{r candidates, eval=FALSE}
calibration_models(single_species = TRUE)
# m0_global:         tp ~ logit_conf
# m1_site_intercept: tp ~ logit_conf + (1 | site)
# m2_site_slope:     tp ~ logit_conf + (logit_conf | site)
```

`uncorrelated = TRUE` optionally adds independent site intercepts and slopes.
One species at one site uses only the global model. Multiple species keep
the original candidate family; with just one site, non-estimable site
random effects are omitted. An explicit `models` list in
`compare_calibration_models()` overrides automatic choice.

The Curiango benchmark originally supplied these three formulas explicitly.
The new automatic family reproduces that comparison to numerical precision
(maximum difference in mean log-loss below 10^-15), with **zero failed
fits**. It is therefore possible to use the benchmark's candidates without
constructing a custom list.

### Predictions on held-out nights

The empirical benchmark uses nested 5 × 5 cross-validation. An outer test
night never enters inner model selection or refitting. The two rules use
identical candidates and partitions. Seed 2026 defines the outer folds;
2027–2031 define the five inner comparisons. This evaluates new nights at
known sites, not transfer to new sites. The following are pooled outer-test
metrics; smaller log-loss and Brier are better.

```{r curiango-metrics, echo=FALSE}
tab <- cur |> filter(scheme=="night") |>
  transmute(Classifier=classifier,Rule=rule,`Log-loss`=fmt(logloss),
            Brier=fmt(brier),AUC=fmt(auc))
knitr::kable(tab)
```

For BirdNET, log-loss is about 3.2% higher under the one-standard-error rule;
for Custom the difference is effectively zero. A paired bootstrap of 2,000
site-night resamples gives:

```{r curiango-uncertainty, echo=FALSE}
tab <- ci |> filter(scheme=="night") |>
 transmute(Classifier=classifier,`New minus AUC log-loss`=fmt(delta_logloss),
           `95% interval`=paste0("[",fmt(logloss_low),", ",fmt(logloss_high),"]"))
knitr::kable(tab)
```

Both intervals include zero. They are conditional on the stored predictions,
not on re-running the whole selection procedure. A sensitivity analysis
holding out whole recordings instead of whole nights favoured `best_auc`
for BirdNET (log-loss difference +0.0129, interval +0.0061 to +0.0198), but
not clearly for Custom. One outer partition was used per protocol. These
metrics condition on score ≥ 0.10 and are not directly comparable with the
article's detector AUCs calculated over a different score range.

### Nightly histories and the cell-status regression

Final fits were applied to the full survey. A site-night is marked detected
when at least one eligible recording has P(TP) ≥ 0.95. These are acoustic
detection histories, not occupancy estimates. Selection using the package's
clip folds and using whole-night folds gives different sensitivities:

```{r curiango-histories, echo=FALSE}
tab <- night |> transmute(Classifier=classifier,
 Folds=ifelse(scheme=="night","Whole nights","Clips"),
 `Detected: AUC`=presences_auc,`Detected: new`=presences_logloss,
 `Nights changed`=changed,`Gained / lost`=paste(gained,lost,sep=" / "))
knitr::kable(tab)
```

The Custom total of 190 versus 188 with clip folds hides **20 changed
nights**, not two: nine gain detection and eleven lose it. Most full-survey
recordings have no manual truth, so these counts measure sensitivity to
analysis choices, not which history is correct. The article's environmental
and occupancy models were not refitted.

The same benchmark exposed a grid-boundary bug in `cell_status()`: a grid
ending at 0.99 missed crossings before a reviewed maximum above 0.99, and
rounding down could include an unreviewed score below the minimum. Including
both observed endpoints corrected **12 of 56 cell statuses**, with no
remaining disagreements against curve endpoints. The core-species decision
still retained Curiango for Custom and excluded it for BirdNET. These are
regression checks, distinct from predictive benchmarks.

## Multispecies: simulation with known truth

No real multispecies validation dataset was available for this benchmark.
The following results are **simulated**, not empirical FrogNet performance.
There are 20 independent seeds per scenario (2026–2045), six sites, eight
species, 36 nights and two candidate windows per site × species × night.
For each replicate, 2,304 windows from the first 24 nights are training data;
1,152 windows from 12 later nights are untouched test data.

The three scenarios are a global logistic score-to-truth relation, random
species intercepts/slopes, and additional site plus site × species
intercepts. Confidence is drawn uniformly between 0.10 and 0.9995; truth is
Bernoulli with the specified probability. Heterogeneous scenarios also have
a shared site-night intercept (SD 0.25) that is omitted from the candidate
models. This is a controlled stress test, not a fitted model of the real
community or classifier recall.

Five-fold selection uses whole training nights and the original five
multispecies candidates m0–m4. Both rules receive the same comparison and
are refitted only on training data. Test labels are used solely to evaluate
predictions and detection histories. The summaries below are means ± SD
across the 20 replicates, **not confidence intervals**.

```{r simulation-summary, echo=FALSE}
tab <- sim |> group_by(scenario,rule) |>
 summarise(`Log-loss`=paste0(fmt(mean(logloss))," ± ",fmt(sd(logloss))),
           Brier=paste0(fmt(mean(brier))," ± ",fmt(sd(brier))),
           .groups="drop") |>
 transmute(Scenario=unname(scenario_names[scenario]),Rule=rule,`Log-loss`,Brier)
knitr::kable(tab)
```

```{r paired-simulation, echo=FALSE, eval=has_plot, fig.cap="Paired test log-loss differences across simulation replicates. Positive values favour best_auc; each point is one simulated dataset, not one clip."}
plot_data <- paired |>
 mutate(scenario=factor(scenario,levels=names(scenario_names),labels=scenario_names))
ggplot2::ggplot(plot_data,ggplot2::aes(scenario,delta_logloss))+
 ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept=0,linetype=2,colour="grey50")+
 ggplot2::geom_boxplot(outlier.shape=NA,width=.45)+
 ggplot2::geom_point(position=ggplot2::position_jitter(width=.10,height=0,seed=2026),alpha=.7)+
 ggplot2::labs(x=NULL,y="Test log-loss: new rule − AUC rule")+
 ggplot2::theme_bw(base_size=11)
```

In the global scenario, `one_se_logloss` selected the global model in
20/20 replicates, versus 13/20 for AUC; the AUC-selected final fit was
singular in five replicates, versus none under the new rule. In the
species-difference scenario the new rule often omitted the varying slope
(14/20 intercept-only choices) and had slightly higher mean test loss.
With site × species differences, both rules selected m4 in 19/20
replicates; one different choice accounts for the largest paired loss
difference. These observations describe this simulation design, not a
universal ranking of the rules. None of the 1,500 cross-validation fits
failed; singular fits were retained or excluded according to each rule.

### Detection histories, core species and matrices

With known window truth we can also compare nightly detections and
community matrices. The history uses P(TP) ≥ 0.95 and k = 1; its truth
reference is at least one true positive among that night's simulated
candidate windows. This is not latent ecological occupancy.

```{r simulation-downstream, echo=FALSE}
tab <- sim |> group_by(scenario,rule) |>
 summarise(`Night precision`=fmt(mean(night_precision,na.rm=TRUE)),
           `Night sensitivity`=fmt(mean(night_sensitivity)),
           `Core species`=sprintf("%.1f",mean(core_species)),
           `Matrix MAE`=fmt(mean(matrix_mae)),.groups="drop") |>
 transmute(Scenario=unname(scenario_names[scenario]),Rule=rule,
           `Night precision`,`Night sensitivity`,`Core species`,`Matrix MAE`)
knitr::kable(tab)
```

`cell_status()` uses training data, `p_min = 0.95` and `min_n = 15`. Matrix
MAE is the mean absolute error of held-out site × month detection frequencies
against simulated truth, using **all eight species on identical axes** for
both rules (`k_min = 1`, `min_nights_month = 1`). It is not an error between
matrices of different dimensions after core-species filtering.

```{r simulation-changes, echo=FALSE}
tab <- changes |> group_by(scenario) |>
 summarise(`Mean changed site-species-nights`=sprintf("%.1f",mean(changed_nights)),
           `Mean core-set Jaccard`=sprintf("%.3f",mean(core_jaccard)),.groups="drop") |>
 transmute(Scenario=unname(scenario_names[scenario]),
           `Mean changed site-species-nights`,`Mean core-set Jaccard`)
knitr::kable(tab)
```

There are 576 test site × species × night combinations per replicate. A
high reliability threshold can yield high precision and low sensitivity;
fewer detected nights must not automatically be interpreted as better
calibration. Core sets need separate inspection even when probability
scores or aggregate counts are similar.

## Computing time

These are elapsed times on one machine, for the current implementation;
they do not establish a speed-up over earlier package versions. They exclude
downloads and rendering. The native Curiango comparisons were repeated three
times with a fixed seed. Simulation timings cover five folds and five
candidates, once for each independently generated dataset. Both rules reuse
the same cross-validation fits.

```{r timings, echo=FALSE}
t <- bench("curiango-timing.csv")
tab <- t |> group_by(classifier) |> summarise(Windows=first(windows),Candidates=first(candidates),
 `Median seconds`=sprintf("%.2f",median(seconds)),
 `Range seconds`=sprintf("%.2f–%.2f",min(seconds),max(seconds)),.groups="drop")
knitr::kable(tab)
d <- bench("multispecies-design.csv")
tab <- d |> group_by(scenario) |> summarise(Replicates=n(),
 `Median CV seconds`=sprintf("%.2f",median(cv_seconds)),
 `IQR seconds`=sprintf("%.2f–%.2f",quantile(cv_seconds,.25),quantile(cv_seconds,.75)),.groups="drop") |>
 mutate(scenario=unname(scenario_names[scenario]))
knitr::kable(tab)
```

The cached `*-session.txt` files record R and dependency versions. Timing
varies with hardware, background load, data and convergence. These small
frequentist fits do not predict the cost of a `brms` refit.

## What you can do, and what did not consistently improve

- Use `fold_group = "source_audio"` or `"night"` when windows share an
  acoustic unit; clip folds can put correlated windows on both sides.
- For one species, let the automatic family use site effects. For exact
  reproduction, provide an explicit candidate list to the comparison.
- Inspect probability scores, singularity, calibration curves and changed
  nights together. Higher AUC or a smaller model alone is not sufficient.
- `one_se_logloss` did not consistently reduce test loss in these datasets.
  A limited simulation and one real species do not justify reversing the
  default, or claiming universal improvement.
- Grouped CV is not leave-one-site-out validation. New sites, sparse
  species, distribution shifts and Bayesian calibration remain outside
  this benchmark. Multispecies empirical validation is still needed.

## Reproduce the results

Run these scripts from a source checkout with `devtools`, `lme4`, `pROC`,
`dplyr`, `tidyr`, `readr` and, for Zenodo downloads, `jsonlite`:

```{r reproduce, eval=FALSE}
# New native single-species family: downloads only two evaluation tables
# if missing and checks their pinned MD5 hashes.
source("dev/benchmarks/curiango-native.R")

# 60 simulated datasets; expensive, opt-in regeneration.
source("dev/benchmarks/multispecies.R")

# Full empirical benchmark: nested CV, recording-level sensitivity,
# histories, diagnostics, paired bootstrap and the original report plots.
source("dev/benchmarks/curiango.R")
```

The simulation script overwrites all its cached tables; regenerate them
after changing the generator, candidate set or design.
The full empirical script writes intermediate output under
`dev/benchmarks/results/curiango/`, separate from the small cached vignette
tables. No benchmark script is run automatically by this article.
